title: Level order, tree input & recursive counts
overview: This module adds breadth-first (level-order) traversal with a queue, and uses the same queue idea to read a whole tree from input, where `-1` means 'no child'. With a real tree in hand you write small recursive functions that count nodes, count leaves and find the height. It ends with STL `pair` and judge practice on traversals.

concepts.explain: Visit the tree level by level, left to right. Put the root in a queue; repeatedly take the front, print it, and push its non-NULL children. The queue makes sure upper levels finish before lower ones.

concepts.term: Reading a tree level by level
concepts.explain: First read the root value. Then, for each node taken from the queue, read two numbers: its left and right child. `-1` means NULL. New real children go into the queue so their children are read later.
Nodes in a tree = nodes on the left + nodes on the right + 1 (the root). An empty tree has 0.
A leaf has both children NULL, so it returns 1. Any other node returns the sum from its two sides, without adding itself.
Height = 1 + the taller of the two subtrees. Decide what a leaf counts as: 0 if you count **edges**, 1 if you count **nodes** (levels). Judges differ, so read the problem.
LeetCode wants the traversal as a `vector<int>`. Pass the vector by reference into a helper and `push_back` where you would have printed.
`pair<A,B>` holds two values, reached with `.first` and `.second`. Create one with `make_pair(a,b)` or `{a,b}`. A `vector<pair<int,int>>` is a neat way to store coordinates or (value, index) data.

files.title: Level-order traversal with a queue
files.what: Uses the hand-built tree from module 17 and prints all four traversals, now each on its own line. The new one, `level_order`, uses a queue.
steps: `preorder`, `inorder`, `postorder` are the recursive functions from before.
`level_order` pushes `root` into `queue<Node*> q`.
Loop: take `f = q.front()`, `pop`, print `f->val`.
Push `f->left` and `f->right` only if they are not NULL.
The loop ends when the queue is empty, meaning every node was printed.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(n) for the queue
files.output_note: The last line is `Level-order traversal: 10 20 30 40 50 60`: level 0 (10), level 1 (20 30), level 2 (40 50 60). Compare with the three depth-first lines above it.
files.watch_out: This `level_order` has no NULL check: calling it with an empty tree pushes NULL and then reads `f->val`, which crashes. The later files add `if(root == NULL)`.

check.q: Why a queue and not a stack for level order?
check.a: A queue hands nodes back in the order they were added, so all nodes of one level come out before their children.

files.title: Read a binary tree from input
files.what: `input_tree` builds a tree from level-order input where `-1` means no child, and `level_order` prints it back to prove the tree is right.
steps: Read the root value; `-1` gives an empty tree (`root = NULL`).
If a root exists, push it into a queue.
Pop a node `p`, read `l` and `r`; create `new Node` for each value that is not `-1`, else use `NULL`.
Attach them as `p->left` and `p->right`, and push the real ones into the queue.
When the queue empties, every node has had its two children read; return `root`.
files.input_note: Root first, then one line with the two children of each real node in level order (20, 30, 40, 50, 60).
files.output_note: `10 20 30 40 50 60` — the level order of the tree just read, so the input was understood correctly.
files.watch_out: Every real node needs its own pair of numbers, even leaves (`-1 -1`). Missing pairs make `cin` fail and the tree comes out wrong.

check.q: How many pairs of numbers follow the root line for a tree with n real nodes?
check.a: n pairs: one pair for every real node, including the root and the leaves.

files.title: Count nodes
files.what: Reads a tree, prints its level order, then prints the number of nodes found by the recursive `count_nodes`.
steps: `input_tree` and `level_order` are the same as in `binary_tree_input.cpp`.
`count_nodes(NULL)` returns 0.
Otherwise it counts the left subtree `l` and right subtree `r`.
It returns `l + r + 1`; the `+1` is the current node.
files.input_note: Level-order tree input with -1 for missing children.
files.output_note: Line 1: the level order. Line 2: `6`, the number of nodes.

check.q: For the node 20 (whose only child is 40), what does `count_nodes` return?
check.a: 2: left gives 1 (node 40), right gives 0, plus 1 for 20 itself.

files.title: Count leaf nodes
files.what: Adds `count_leaf_nodes`, which returns 1 for a node with no children and otherwise adds the leaf counts of both sides.
steps: `count_leaf_nodes(NULL)` returns 0.
If both `left` and `right` are NULL, the node is a leaf: return 1.
Otherwise return the leaves on the left plus the leaves on the right (the node itself is not added).
`main` reads the tree and prints the level order and then a count.
files.input_note: Level-order tree input with -1 for missing children.
files.output_note: You see `6`, not the leaf count. The real leaf count for this tree is 3 (40, 50, 60).
files.watch_out: Bug: `main` prints `count_nodes(root)` instead of `count_leaf_nodes(root)`, so the new function is never used. Fix: `cout << count_leaf_nodes(root) << endl;`.

check.q: Why does the leaf case need its own check before the recursive calls?
check.a: Without it a leaf would return 0 + 0 = 0, since both its children are NULL, and no leaf would ever be counted.

files.title: Maximum height of a tree
files.what: Adds `max_height`, which measures height in **edges**: a leaf has height 0 and each parent adds 1 to its taller child.
steps: `max_height(NULL)` returns 0.
A leaf also returns 0 (no edges below it).
Otherwise compute `l` and `r` for the two subtrees.
Return `max(l, r) + 1`.
`main` prints the level order, the node count, then the height.
files.input_note: Level-order tree input with -1 for missing children.
files.output_note: Lines: level order, `6` nodes, and `2` for the height: the longest path 10 → 20 → 40 has 2 edges.
files.watch_out: Returning 0 for both NULL and a leaf makes a node with only one child still count correctly here (0 + 1), but the function gives 0 for both an empty tree and a single node. The Code360 version below counts nodes instead and would print 3.

check.q: What does `max_height` return for a straight chain of 4 nodes?

files.title: STL pair and vector of pairs
files.what: Shows how to create pairs with `make_pair` and `{}`, print `.first` and `.second`, and store pairs in a vector. The last part tries to read `n` pairs from input.
steps: `p1 = make_pair(2, 3)` and `p2 = {2, 3}` build the same pair.
`pair<string,int>` shows the two parts can have different types.
`v.push_back(make_pair(1, 2))` stores pairs in a `vector`, printed with `v[i].first` and `v[i].second`.
Finally it reads `n` and fills a `vector<pair<int,int>>` of size `n` with `cin >> v[i].first >> v[i].second`.
files.input_note: n, then n lines with two integers each.
files.output_note: The program does not compile, so nothing is printed. When fixed, it prints `2 3`, `2 3`, `Hello 3`, `1 2`, `3 4`; the pairs read at the end are stored but not printed.
files.watch_out: Compile error: `v` is declared twice in `main` (`vector<pair<int, int>> v;` and later `v(n)`). Fix: rename the second one, e.g. `vector<pair<int, int>> v2(n);`.

check.q: How do you read the second value of the 3rd pair in `vector<pair<int,int>> v`?

files.title: LeetCode 144 - Binary Tree Preorder Traversal
files.what: Returns the pre-order of a tree as a vector. A helper `preorder` fills the vector passed by reference.
steps: `preorderTraversal` makes an empty `result` and calls `preorder(root, result)`.
The helper returns on `NULL`.
It pushes `node->val` first, then recurses left, then right.
Because `result` is passed with `&`, all calls add to the same vector.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(h) plus the output
files.input_note: The tree in level order with -1 for a missing child. This is LeetCode's example `[1,null,2,3]`: root 1, right child 2, and 3 is the left child of 2.
files.output_note: `preorder = [1,2,3]`, which matches LeetCode's expected answer: the root 1 first, then the right subtree 2 → 3.
files.watch_out: Forgetting the `&` on `result` in the helper would leave the returned vector empty, because each call would fill its own copy.

check.q: What would go wrong if the helper took `vector<int> result` without `&`?
check.a: Each call would fill its own copy, and the vector returned by `preorderTraversal` would stay empty.

files.title: LeetCode 94 - Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
files.what: Same pattern as the pre-order solution, but the `push_back` sits between the two recursive calls.
steps: Create `result` and call `inorder(root, result)`.
Return on `NULL`.
Recurse left, push `node->val`, recurse right.
Return `result`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(h) plus the output
files.input_note: The tree in level order with -1 for a missing child. This is LeetCode's example `[1,null,2,3]`: root 1, right child 2, and 3 is the left child of 2.
files.output_note: `inorder = [1,3,2]`, which matches LeetCode's expected answer: 1 has no left side, so it comes first, then 2's left child 3, then 2.

check.q: Which single line moves when you turn this into a pre-order solution?

files.title: LeetCode 145 - Binary Tree Postorder Traversal
files.what: Post-order into a vector: both recursive calls first, then `push_back` the node.
steps: Create `result` and call `postorder(root, result)`.
Return on `NULL`.
Recurse left, recurse right, then push `node->val`.
Return `result`.
files.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(h) plus the output
files.input_note: The tree in level order with -1 for a missing child. This is LeetCode's example `[1,null,2,3]`: root 1, right child 2, and 3 is the left child of 2.
files.output_note: `postorder = [3,2,1]`, which matches LeetCode's expected answer: the children come before their parents, so the root 1 is last.

check.q: Which element is always last in the returned vector?

files.title: Code360 - Level Order Traversal
files.what: The queue-based level order from the lesson, but values are collected into a `vector<int>` instead of printed.
steps: Return an empty vector if `root` is NULL.
Push `root` into a queue of node pointers.
Pop the front, `push_back` its `val` into `result`.
Push its non-NULL left and right children.
Return `result` when the queue is empty.
files.input_note: The tree in level order with -1 for a missing child (the Code360 input style). It is the lesson tree: 10 has children 20 and 30, 20 has left child 40, 30 has children 50 and 60.
files.output_note: `level order: 10 20 30 40 50 60`, one level after another: 10, then 20 30, then 40 50 60.
files.watch_out: Without the `root == NULL` check, a NULL pointer would go into the queue and reading `current->val` would crash.

check.q: Why check `root == NULL` before pushing it?
check.a: Otherwise a NULL pointer enters the queue and reading `current->val` crashes.

files.title: Code360 - Count Leaf Nodes
files.what: The recursive leaf counter from the lesson, written for the judge's `BinaryTreeNode<int>`.
steps: NULL → 0.
No left and no right child → 1.
Otherwise return leaves on the left plus leaves on the right.
files.input_note: The tree in level order with -1 for a missing child (the Code360 input style). It is the lesson tree: 10 has children 20 and 30, 20 has left child 40, 30 has children 50 and 60.

check.q: How many leaves does a perfect binary tree with 3 levels have?

files.title: Code360 - Left Sum
files.what: Adds up the values of every node that is a **left child** of some node. A level-order walk looks at each node's left child and adds it to `sum`.
steps: Return 0 for an empty tree; keep `sum` as `long long` to avoid overflow.
BFS with a queue starting at `root`.
For each `current`, if `current->left` exists, add its `data` to `sum` and push it.
Push `current->right` if it exists, without adding it.
Return `sum` when the queue is empty.
files.input_note: The tree in level order with -1 for a missing child (the Code360 input style). It is the lesson tree: 10 has children 20 and 30, 20 has left child 40, 30 has children 50 and 60.
files.output_note: `left sum = 110`: the left children are 20, 40 and 50, and 20 + 40 + 50 = 110.
files.watch_out: The root is never a left child, so its value is never added. Keep `sum` as `long long` because the total can be large.

check.q: Why is the value added when looking at the parent, not when the node itself is popped?
check.a: A popped node does not know whether it is a left or right child; its parent does.

files.title: Code360 - Height of a Binary Tree
files.what: Height counted in **nodes**: a leaf has height 1, and each parent is 1 more than its taller child.
steps: NULL → 0.
Leaf → 1.
Otherwise return `max(left height, right height) + 1`.
files.input_note: The tree in level order with -1 for a missing child (the Code360 input style). It is the lesson tree: 10 has children 20 and 30, 20 has left child 40, 30 has children 50 and 60.
files.output_note: `height = 3`: the tree has three levels, and this version counts nodes. `get_max_height.cpp` counts edges and gives 2 for the same tree.
files.watch_out: Judges measure height differently. This one counts nodes (a leaf is 1). `get_max_height.cpp` counts edges (a leaf is 0).

check.q: Is the leaf check actually needed in this version?
check.a: No. With NULL → 0, a leaf already gives max(0,0)+1 = 1. It only makes the intent clear.

recap: Level order = BFS with a queue: pop, use, push non-NULL children.
The same queue loop reads a tree from input, with `-1` meaning no child.
Count nodes: left + right + 1. Count leaves: 1 at a leaf, else left + right.
Height: max(left, right) + 1; decide whether a leaf is 0 (edges) or 1 (nodes).
For judges, pass the result vector by reference and `push_back` instead of printing.

check_yourself.q: Write the input (with -1s) for a tree with root 5, left child 3, and no right child.
In a tree of n nodes, what is the most memory the level-order queue can need?
check_yourself.a: About the width of the widest level, which can be up to about n/2 — so O(n).

check_yourself.q: A tree is a single node. What is its height in edges and in nodes?
Which traversal would you use to print a tree row by row?

body: Module 17 gave you three ways to walk a tree, and all three dive to the bottom before they come back up. Pre-order on the tree below prints `10 20 40 30 50 60`: it goes all the way down the left side before it even looks at 30.
But look at the picture and ask the question a person would ask about it: what is on the top row, then the second row, then the third row?
The answer you want is `10`, then `20 30`, then `40 50 60`. None of the three traversals produces that, because recursion always finishes one child completely before it starts the other.

You could get it the slow way. Work out the depth of every node, then make one pass printing only the nodes at depth 0, another pass for depth 1, another for depth 2. A tree 20 levels deep would mean 20 passes over the whole tree.

A clerk in a post office would not do that. They would keep a waiting line: write the root on the line, take the person at the front off the line, deal with them, and put their two children at the back. That line is a queue, exactly the queue of Module 14, and the order it hands nodes back is level order.
What is new is only what the queue holds. Until now your queues held numbers or characters; here every item is a `Node*`, a pointer to a node. The loop itself is four lines:

Push a child only if it exists. If you push a NULL, the next round reads `f->val` through it and the program crashes. The first file also forgets the empty tree, and the files after it add `if(root == NULL) return;` at the top.

The same queue solves a second problem. So far every tree was built by hand, one `new Node` and one assignment at a time, which is fine for six nodes and hopeless for a judge. Let the input describe the tree instead. Read the root value, push it, then take a node off the queue and read two numbers: its left child and its right child, where `-1` means no child. Real children are pushed, so their own children get read later, in the same order.

That input describes the tree in the picture above. Notice that every node that comes off the queue reads exactly two numbers, leaves included, so each leaf needs its own `-1 -1`. An empty tree is a single `-1`.
intro.trace:
10          <- the root
20 30       <- children of 10
40 -1       <- children of 20
50 60       <- children of 30
-1 -1       <- children of 40
-1 -1       <- children of 50
-1 -1       <- children of 60

body: With a real tree in hand, the counting questions all have one shape: ask the left child, ask the right child, combine the two answers, and stop at NULL. You never walk the tree yourself.

Leaves use the same shape with a different rule: a node with no children returns 1, any other node returns left plus right and does not count itself, which gives 3 here (40, 50 and 60). Height is `max(left, right) + 1`, which gives 3 on this tree if a leaf counts as 1. Some judges count edges instead and want a leaf to be 0, so read the problem before you submit.

The programs below work through all of it: the queue traversal, the input builder, the three counting functions, `pair` for carrying two values at once, and judge versions of the traversals you already know.
intro.trace:
count(x) = count(left) + count(right) + 1

count(40) = 0 + 0 + 1 = 1
count(20) = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2
count(50) = 1   count(60) = 1
count(30) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3
count(10) = 2 + 3 + 1 = 6

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: the queue reading the tree row by row
body: This is the trace above with the tree drawn next to it. The node in `[ ]` is the one just taken off the front of the queue; its children join at the back.
Watch the queue line only: it always holds the nodes waiting their turn, and they are always in top-to-bottom, left-to-right order. That is the whole reason this prints the tree row by row.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows or Play - one pop per frame

frames.label: Before the loop starts, `q.push(root)` puts 10 on the waiting line. Nothing is printed yet.
Take the front node off, print it, and push its children at the back. 10 is printed and 20 and 30 join the line. The first row is finished already.
Front of the line is 20. Print it, then push its children - it only has a left child, so only 40 joins, at the back behind 30.
Now 30. Print it and push both of its children, 50 and 60, behind 40. The second row is printed, and the queue now holds the whole third row.
Take 40. It is a leaf, so nothing joins the line. Notice 40 had to wait behind 30 even though it is further down the left side - pre-order would have printed it long ago.
Take 50, also a leaf. From here the line can only get shorter, because nothing new is being pushed.
Take 60, the last node. It is pushed nothing, printed, and the queue is empty.
The queue is empty so `while(!q.empty())` stops. Read the printed line in the groups the tree made: 10, then 20 30, then 40 50 60 - the tree row by row, in one pass, with no recursion at all.
